claims.text: Directional solidification can induce a columnar grain structure in high-entropy alloys.
The induced columnar grains can be aligned with the dominant heat-flow direction.
Directional solidification can be implemented through plasma arc additive manufacturing with controlled oscillation.
Conventional casting or non-directional additive processing produces an equiaxed or randomly dendritic HEA microstructure.
Directional solidification will improve the heat-transfer capability of an HEA intermediate layer.
Directional solidification will preserve mechanical integrity under plasma-facing reactor intermediate-layer conditions.
The expected benefit should hold at approximately 500–1200 °C under high heat flux, irradiation, and mechanical loading.
The intervention develops aligned columnar grains.
The columnar microstructure contains coherent grain boundaries.
Aligned columnar grains and their boundaries reduce intergranular scattering of heat carriers.
Directional grain alignment minimizes interfacial scattering of electrons and phonons and creates continuous thermal-conduction pathways.
A coherent microstructure preserves mechanical strength by maintaining load-bearing connectivity under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Directional solidification should increase thermal conductivity by approximately 10–20% relative to the conventional equiaxed material.
The thermal-conductivity improvement should occur without a significant loss of mechanical integrity.
A conventional HEA intermediate layer with a random grain structure has lower heat-transfer efficiency.
The benefit depends on the columnar structure remaining stable during prolonged high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
Microstructural degradation or coarsening could reduce the heat-transfer improvement.
A controlled comparison will use conventionally cast samples and directionally solidified samples exposed to the same simulated plasma-facing conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if the directionally solidified material fails to achieve a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase of at least 10%, or if its strength or ductility is compromised beyond acceptable limits.
